criteria.note: The thesis for "gluten in korean food" — that the gluten lives in the fermented condiments, not the visible dish — lands in the second paragraph, well inside 200 words, and the condiment table follows immediately.

Keyword present in both; title is 35 chars and still 55 with the rendered ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix, description is ~153 chars, and beyond the keyword itself the two share no phrasing — the description adds 밀떡, the barley gap and the swaps.

Headings state conclusions rather than label topics ("The allergen line only covers wheat", "Noodles: mostly wheat, with two bright spots", "The good news: control the condiments, reclaim the cuisine"), so a heading-only skim reproduces the argument end to end.
Three distinct internal destinations (label-reading guide, restaurant list, pillar Korea guide), each placed where the reader actually hits the limit of this page rather than bolted onto the end.

All three FAQ answers are established in the body — soy sauce by the condiment table, tteokbokki by the 밀떡/sauce/eomuk triple-check, dangmyeon by the noodles section plus the shared-wok caveat in the celiac section — and each reads standalone.

Dated, located, first-hand detail throughout: a named anchor restaurant closing in Hannam and still closed in summer 2026, a monil2 house visit in Yeonnam, a loaf bought online whose label was quietly renamed, and a relative who brews jip-ganjang — including a self-corrected past error about 떡.

Korean terms are consistently romanised (양조간장 yangjo-ganjang, 밀떡 mil-tteok, 원재료명 wonjaeryomyeong), the three distinct wheat routes into gochujang are named (소맥분/밀쌀/양조간장), and a specific product (Sempio 양조간장 501) and regulation table (별표 2) are cited precisely enough to check.

The two claims that carry the most weight — soy sauce composition and the allergen-line gap — are linked to primary sources (Sempio's own product page, the MFDS 식품등의표시기준) each with an August 2026 retrieval date and a note that the standard is amended.

A dedicated method-limits paragraph states this is not a brand survey and that a label cannot establish freedom from trace gluten, the GFCO search is framed as an unproven absence, the Goraesa lead is explicitly not a clearance, and no commercial link appears anywhere.

findings.why: The update note at the top promises the piece "named the wheat-free condiments actually in our kitchen," but the substitution section gives a category (tamari) plus stores, not a product a reader could look up — the same specificity standard the piece applies to Sempio 501 elsewhere.
findings.fix: Name the exact tamari bottle and the gochujang currently in the kitchen (brand + product line + the 원재료명 wording you read), or reword the update note to say the piece names condiment *categories* rather than products.

findings.quote: Japanese-style Korean curry blocks are thickened with wheat flour.
findings.why: The two load-bearing claims (soy sauce, allergen line) are linked to primary sources with retrieval dates, but the whole "Second-tier hidden sources" list — curry roux, fish cake binder, sausage filler, dressings — is asserted with no attribution at all, so a reader has nothing to verify against.
findings.fix: Link one manufacturer ingredient page per bullet (e.g. an Ottogi curry block product page, one eomuk product page) with a retrieval date, the same pattern already used for Sempio.

findings.quote: Usually not, and the rice cakes are only part of the answer.
findings.why: Every FAQ answer is supported by the body, but this one runs ~130 words; Google truncates FAQ rich results well before that, so the useful part (three separate checks: tteok, sauce, fish cake) risks being cut off.
findings.fix: Front-load each answer with a 1–2 sentence standalone verdict, then the qualifiers — e.g. lead with "Usually not: the sauce is gochujang-based, the fish cake is wheat-bound, and the tteok itself may be 밀떡 (wheat)."

criteria.note: Safety-critical claims are sourced (Sempio, MFDS) or explicitly marked as unverified leads, but a handful of category-level food facts carry neither a source nor an observation marker.
criteria.evidence_quote: home-brewed soy sauce, which is soybeans and salt without the wheat that goes into commercial 양조간장

criteria.note: Product names (Sempio 501, Goraesa, GFCO, monil2 house), the MFDS standard and all dates are checkable, internally consistent, and the piece explicitly says it removed an unsourceable percentage figure.

A dedicated paragraph states the method (reading 원재료명 on products they cook with plus linked sources) and names exactly what it cannot establish — brand coverage, reformulation, and trace gluten from shared equipment.
No absolute safety claims, cross-contamination named at pan/wok/fryer/utensil level in body and FAQs, and celiac risk is explicitly held to a stricter standard than the author's NCGS reality.
Both external sources carry August 2026 retrieval dates, the MFDS standard is flagged as amended regularly, and reformulation-without-notice is stated as a standing limit.
The load-bearing labelling fact is correct — 밀 is mandatory, 보리 and 호밀 are not — and the Korean terms and product categories (밀떡/쌀떡, 당면, 밀쌀, 집간장, 알레르기 유발물질) are used accurately.

The reader gets the exact hangul strings to scan for, a linked manufacturer page and the regulation itself, a linked four-step label method, and an open invitation to correct the GFCO-equivalent claim.

findings.quote: we learned to say **"밀가루 알러지"** (wheat allergy) rather than "gluten-free."
findings.why: The article establishes two sections earlier that barley is not a mandatory allergen and 'appears in gochujang, in malt syrups, in 보리차'. A celiac reader who uses the recommended script gets a kitchen check for wheat only, which does not cover the barley route the piece itself identifies as the most common way a careful reader gets caught. Not blocking — the script is framed as a way to make staff check, not as a safety guarantee, and the celiac section separately tells readers to assume shared equipment.
findings.fix: Add a half-sentence to the restaurant script noting that for celiac the phrase should extend to barley, e.g. suggest '밀가루·보리 알러지' or a written card covering 밀/보리/호밀, and cross-reference the barley gap section.

findings.quote: home-brewed soy sauce, which is soybeans and salt without the wheat that goes into commercial 양조간장
findings.why: This and several sibling claims (curry roux thickened with wheat flour, wheat as a common sausage binder, dangmyeon as sweet potato starch, tamari stocked at named retailers) are neither sourced nor explicitly marked as the authors' own observation, and the jip-ganjang and dangmyeon ones point in the permissive direction. The stated method paragraph covers 'the condiment map below', not the second-tier list or the substitutes section.
findings.fix: Either extend the method framing to cover the second-tier list and substitutes explicitly ('these are our working defaults, not label reads'), or attach a source to the permissive ones — particularly jip-ganjang composition and the tamari retail availability.
